meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'Everybody Needs Somebody to Love'?
meta.ogDescription: Not The Blues Brothers. Solomon Burke recorded it for Atlantic on 28 May 1964 and it peaked at No. 58. The 1980 film version is a cover.

answer.label: Not a Blues Brothers original — a 1964 Solomon Burke single on Atlantic
answer.originalArtistDates: 1940–2010 · American soul singer, "King of Rock 'n' Soul"
answer.sourceLine: Ask most people where “Everybody Needs Somebody to Love” comes from and the answer is Jake and Elwood Blues in the 1980 film. The record they are thinking of is a cover. Solomon Burke recorded the song on 28 May 1964, produced by Bert Berns, and Atlantic issued it as a single that July; Burke shares the writing credit with Berns and Jerry Wexler. The original was not a hit — it charted for eight weeks and stalled at No. 58 on the US pop chart — and it took The Rolling Stones, Wilson Pickett and finally The Blues Brothers to turn it into a standard.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Atlantic
original.released: Issued as a 7-inch single on Atlantic Records in July 1964, catalogue number 2241, backed with “Looking for My Baby.” The master was cut at a session on 28 May 1964 produced by Bert Berns.
original.charted: Peaked at No. 58 on the US pop chart, with eight weeks on the survey — a minor showing. The song's best chart result came later, from Wilson Pickett's cover: No. 29 pop and No. 19 R&B in early 1967.
original.writer: Bert Berns, Solomon Burke and Jerry Wexler
original.cover: The Blues Brothers — John Belushi and Dan Aykroyd — performed it in the 1980 film, and it appears on the Atlantic soundtrack album released 20 June 1980. That album reached No. 13 on the Billboard 200 and was certified platinum in the US. A UK single reissue of the recording, backed with “Minnie the Moocher,” peaked at No. 12 in 1990.
trail: Atlantic put it out in July 1964 as a single and it went almost nowhere — No. 58, eight weeks — per the song's recording history ↗.
The Rolling Stones recorded it in January 1965 for The Rolling Stones No. 2, with a version also turning up on the US album The Rolling Stones, Now! — documented here ↗.
Wilson Pickett's 1966 cover, from The Wicked Pickett, gave the song its highest chart placing: No. 29 pop and No. 19 R&B in early 1967.
The Blues Brothers took it into the 1980 film and onto the Atlantic soundtrack album ↗, which reached No. 13 on the Billboard 200 — on the same label that had released Burke's single.

authors.name: Solomon Burke
authors.heading: Solomon Burke
authors.bio: Burke was one of the founding figures of 1960s soul, a preacher's-pulpit voice who moved between gospel phrasing, country balladry and hard R&B without ever sounding like he had changed lanes. Jerry Wexler, who ran his sessions at Atlantic, called him the greatest male soul singer of all time, and Burke's run of 32 Atlantic singles helped keep the label solvent through the decade. He performed crowned and caped from 1963 onward, billing himself “King Solomon” and the “King of Rock 'n' Soul.” He cut this song on 28 May 1964 and later maintained he had written it alone, from a march he remembered from childhood church offerings, before being talked into sharing the credit.

authors.name: The Blues Brothers
authors.heading: The Blues Brothers
authors.metaLine: John Belushi & Dan Aykroyd · film soundtrack released 20 June 1980 on Atlantic
authors.bio: Belushi and Aykroyd built the Blues Brothers out of genuine affection for exactly this catalogue, and they hired the players to prove it. Their version of the song appears in the 1980 film and on the Atlantic soundtrack album, which reached No. 13 on the Billboard 200 and went platinum in the United States. There is nothing dishonest about the record — it is a loving, deliberate revival, on the same label that put out Burke's single. The only error is chronological: audiences met the song here first and assumed it started here.

authors.name: Bert Berns
authors.heading: Bert Berns
authors.metaLine: American songwriter and record producer · produced the 1964 Atlantic session
authors.bio: Berns is the third name on the credit alongside Burke and Jerry Wexler, and he produced the 28 May 1964 session that put the song on tape. He was one of the great crossover writer-producers of the era, equally at home with soul singers and British beat groups — which is part of why the song reached The Rolling Stones so quickly. Burke's own account is that Berns and Wexler reshaped the tempo of what he brought in, and that the shared credit followed from that.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong starting point
misattribution.intro: The 1980 film is where most people met this song, so the film is where most people think it began. The recording history says otherwise, and it is not close.

items.why: Belushi and Aykroyd's version appears in the 1980 film and on the Atlantic soundtrack released 20 June 1980. It is a cover of a record Atlantic had already released in 1964 — and it was not even the first famous cover.
Recorded 28 May 1964 at Atlantic, produced by Bert Berns, and released as a single in July 1964 as Atlantic 2241 backed with “Looking for My Baby.” It charted for eight weeks and peaked at No. 58.

items.who: Bert Berns, Solomon Burke and Jerry Wexler
items.why: All three names are on the credit. Burke later said he wrote it alone, from a march he remembered from church, and was persuaded to share the credit with his producer and his label boss. That dispute is about authorship, not about who recorded it first.
Often forgotten in this argument: Pickett's version, from The Wicked Pickett, reached No. 29 pop and No. 19 R&B in early 1967 — the song's strongest chart performance, and long before the film.

misattribution.truthLine: Solomon Burke recorded it first, in May 1964. Everything else — the Stones, Pickett, the Blues Brothers — is a cover.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The interesting question is not why The Blues Brothers version is famous — it comes attached to a hit film — but why there was so little competition for the memory. Burke's single simply did not travel. It charted for eight weeks and peaked at No. 58 on the US pop chart, which means most listeners in 1964 never heard it at all. A song that never lodged as a hit leaves no impression for a later version to displace.

What happened instead is that the song became famous through its covers, in stages. The Rolling Stones recorded it in January 1965 and put it on The Rolling Stones No. 2; Wilson Pickett cut it for The Wicked Pickett in 1966 and took it to No. 29 pop and No. 19 R&B, the song's best chart showing by some distance. By the time Belushi and Aykroyd got to it, it was already a standard with no single owner in the public mind — and a film gave it one.
detailsBody: 28 May 1964 — Solomon Burke records the song for Atlantic, produced by Bert Berns. Writing credit: Berns, Burke and Jerry Wexler.
July 1964 — Atlantic issues it as a single, catalogue 2241, backed with “Looking for My Baby.” It charts for eight weeks and peaks at No. 58 on the US pop chart.
January 1965 — The Rolling Stones record their version, which appears on The Rolling Stones No. 2 in the UK and on the US album The Rolling Stones, Now!
1966 — Wilson Pickett records it for The Wicked Pickett; his version reaches No. 29 pop and No. 19 R&B in early 1967, the song's biggest chart result.
20 June 1980 — The Blues Brothers version appears on the Atlantic soundtrack to the film. The album reaches No. 13 on the Billboard 200 and is certified platinum in the US.
1989–1990 — The Blues Brothers recording is issued as a UK single; a 1990 reissue backed with “Minnie the Moocher” peaks at No. 12 in the UK.
context.pull: The original never charted high enough to be remembered, so the cover had nothing to displace.
